description: We are a curious and collaborative team passionate about science, technology, innovation, and problem-solving. We bring different skills, ideas, and perspectives together to explore challenges and create practical solutions. Through the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we aim to learn, experiment, use space data creatively, and build an innovative solution with meaningful real-world impact.
summary:
The Ones Who Remained is an interactive, story-driven space research experience created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026’s “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” challenge. At its centre is ECHO, a website inspired by the research assistant in our story about Mira, a young explorer introduced to NASA’s legacy hardware by Dr. Voss.

ECHO lets visitors explore the Moon, Mars, and deep space through highly detailed, zoomable 3D visualizations. Markers identify locations associated with spacecraft, landers, rovers, and other mission hardware that remained after their active service. Selecting a marker reveals an image and a clear explanation of the object’s purpose, mission history, scientific contributions, and lasting significance. Visitors can move from a broad view of each environment to focused information about individual artifacts, learning at their own pace.

Rather than treating retired hardware as forgotten debris, our project presents it as evidence of human ingenuity and scientific progress. The experience supports Mira’s fictional journey while also standing alone as an accessible educational research tool. By combining engaging visuals, interactive discovery, and NASA mission research, we hope to inspire students and space enthusiasts to appreciate how yesterday’s explorers continue to inform tomorrow’s missions.
details:
Project Details: THE ONES WHO STAYED

What does it do and how does it work? "THE ONES WHO STAYED" is a cinematic, interactive 3D web experience that serves as an educational archive of humanity's greatest deep-space artifacts. Operating entirely in the browser, the application allows users to encounter iconic spacecraft (such as Voyager 1, the James Webb Space Telescope, and the Perseverance Rover) floating in a responsive, particle-driven starfield.

The core feature is the 3D "Exploded-View" Disassembler. With a single click, users can smoothly expand the spacecraft into their constituent components. By selecting individual parts—like Voyager's Golden Record or JWST's primary mirror—a glassmorphic inspection drawer reveals the component's function, historical backstory, aerospace contractors, and technical specifications. Finally, the app features an "Arcade Rec Room" with two HTML5 Canvas minigames (an orbital gravity-assist simulator and an orbital debris catcher) to gamify the physics of space exploration.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact? Spacecraft engineering is often locked behind dense technical documentation and blueprints that are inaccessible to the general public. This project bridges that gap. By breaking down monumental machines into understandable, interactive pieces, we demystify aerospace engineering.

The intended impact is deeply educational and inspirational. We want to honor the engineers and scientists who built these machines—"the ones who stayed" on Earth while their creations ventured into the void. By presenting this data in a highly polished, gamified, and visually stunning format, we aim to inspire the next generation of STEM students to see spacecraft not just as scientific tools, but as human triumphs.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? To ensure maximum accessibility, instant load times, and cross-platform compatibility, the entire application was engineered as a highly optimized, single-file web application without relying on heavy external 3D asset files.

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, Modern JavaScript (ES6+ Modules).
  • Graphics & 3D Engine: Three.js / WebGL for the 3D rendering loop, implementing procedural geometry, wireframe overlays, and UnrealBloom post-processing for a neon-cinematic aesthetic.
  • 2D Graphics & Gaming: HTML5 <canvas> API for the ambient starfield and the custom arcade physics engine.
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS (via CDN) for rapid, responsive layout structuring and glassmorphism UI effects.
  • Animation & Audio: GSAP (GreenSock) for silky-smooth camera easing and transitions, and the native Web Audio API for synthesizing procedural sound effects (synths, swooshes) without external audio files.

How is your project creative? Instead of importing massive .gltf or .obj files that require long loading screens and complex server setups, we took a highly creative, programmatic approach. Every spacecraft in the application is an "Educational Reconstruction" built entirely from procedural Three.js primitives (boxes, cylinders, planes) arranged via code. We applied custom shaders, edge geometry (blueprints), and bloom lighting to make these primitive shapes look like high-tech, futuristic schematics.

Furthermore, the narrative progression—Encounter → Look Inside → Inspect → Learn → Play—transforms a standard database into a storytelling journey, wrapping hard data in a premium, documentary-style atmosphere.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility: We implemented a prefers-reduced-motion media query check. If a user's system requests reduced motion, the app automatically disables the floating animations and instantaneous camera zooms, opting for static transitions.
  • Performance: The Three.js render loop is tightly controlled. We dynamically clean up memory (disposing of geometries and materials) when switching between spacecraft to prevent memory leaks in the browser.
  • Responsiveness: The UI is built to scale flawlessly from ultra-wide desktop monitors down to mobile touch screens, implementing touch-specific event listeners for the arcade games and 3D orbit controls.
  • Scientific Accuracy: While the 3D models are illustrative reconstructions, the data (mass, power, materials, contractors) was rigorously researched from public NASA archives, ensuring the educational value remains intact.
